titleEn: Praise the LORD from the heavens
progression: | C G | Am Em | F C | G C |
intro: Fourteen verses, one of the five Halleluyah psalms that close the book and are said every morning in Pesukei deZimra, so a beginner hears this one daily. Its shape is a single instruction stretched over the whole text: praise Him, followed by a list of everything that exists, in order. Verses 1 to 6 summon the heavens, verses 7 to 14 summon the earth, and each half stops at the same refrain, let them praise the name of the LORD, in verse 5 and verse 13. For a learner the value is one verb in three forms: the plain plural imperative hal'lu four times, the same imperative with the object suffix him, hal'luhu, six times, and the jussive yehal'lu, let them praise, opening both refrains. Nothing in the psalm explains how a sea creature or a mountain is supposed to comply.

stichs.en: Praise Yah.
Praise the LORD from the heavens;
praise Him in the heights.

verses.summary: The call is issued twice before anything is named, and the location comes before the audience: from the heavens, in the heights. The psalm is organised by address rather than by argument.

stichs.en: Praise Him, all His messengers;
praise Him, all His hosts.

verses.summary: The first two groups called are the ones that already do this. Angels and hosts are the easy case, and putting them first makes everything that follows look like the same instruction.

stichs.en: Praise Him, sun and moon;
praise Him, all stars of light.

verses.summary: Sun, moon and stars are addressed as subjects who can be told to do something. In the surrounding cultures they were gods; here they are entries on a roll call, filed between angels and water.

stichs.en: Praise Him, heavens of heavens,
and the waters that are above the heavens.

verses.summary: The highest and strangest items on the list: a noun doubled in construct to mean the sky beyond the sky, and the water that the creation account places over it. The descent begins after this verse.

stichs.en: Let them praise the name of the LORD,
for He commanded and they were created.

verses.summary: The first refrain, and the only reason the psalm offers for the command: they exist because of an order. A thing that came into being by a word is being asked to answer in the same currency.

stichs.en: He set them up for ever and always;
He gave a limit, and it does not pass.

verses.summary: Permanence and a boundary in one breath. What the last clause says is disputed: either the limit itself never lapses, or nothing that was made ever crosses it.

stichs.en: Praise the LORD from the earth,
sea creatures and all deeps;

verses.summary: The second half opens by mirroring verse 1 exactly, with earth in place of heavens, and the first things named are the lowest and the least domesticated.

stichs.en: fire and hail, snow and vapour,
storm wind that carries out His word;

verses.summary: Weather in one line, then the clause that governs it: doing His word. The storm is not praising in spite of being destructive, it praises by doing what it was told.

stichs.en: the mountains and all hills,
fruit trees and all cedars;

verses.summary: From weather to terrain to what grows on it. Fruit trees and cedars divide the plant world into what feeds people and what does not, and both are summoned on the same terms.

stichs.en: the wild animals and all cattle,
creeping things and winged birds;

verses.summary: Animals in six words, sorted the way the creation account sorts them: wild, domestic, creeping, winged. Nothing on this list is chosen for being impressive.

stichs.en: kings of the earth and all peoples,
princes and all judges of the earth;

verses.summary: Humanity enters at the top, with the people who normally receive praise rather than give it, and they are placed on the same list as hail.

stichs.en: young men and young women too,
old men together with boys.

verses.summary: The ranking collapses in a single verse. Age and office stop mattering the moment the list reaches people who hold neither.

stichs.en: Let them praise the name of the LORD,
for His name alone is exalted;
His splendour is over earth and heaven.

verses.summary: The second refrain, and this time the reason given is not creation but height. The last clause puts both halves of the psalm, earth and heaven, under one word.

stichs.en: He has raised a horn for His people,
praise for all His faithful,
for the children of Israel, a people near to Him.
Praise Yah.

verses.summary: The last verse narrows from everything that exists to one people. A horn is raised, a praise is assigned, and the psalm closes on the two words it opened with.

pardes.body: Two halves that mirror each other down to the wording. Verse 1 says from the heavens, {{1.6}}; verse 7 says from the earth, {{7.4}}, with the same verb and the same preposition in front of it. Each half is a roll call and each stops at the same refrain, verse 5 and verse 13. The order inside them is spatial: down from the heavens of heavens and the waters above, through angels and lights, then across to the deeps and their creatures, up through weather, mountains, trees, animals, and finally people, who are themselves ranked from kings down to children until the ranking stops mattering. The list ends at one people standing near. Nothing in the psalm asks whether a cedar can obey.

Verse 4 shows the language making a superlative out of nothing but repetition: {{4.1}} and {{4.2}} are the same noun twice, in construct, and the phrase means the highest sky there is. Hebrew builds several superlatives this way and this is the cleanest example in the psalter. Verse 6 carries a real dispute. The clause {{6.5}} with {{6.6}} has no expressed subject, so it says either that the limit He gave never lapses, or that nothing crosses it; JPS 1917 chose the second and rendered it as a decree that shall not be transgressed. Verse 8 has a rare word, {{8.3}}, translated as vapour by JPS 1917 and as smoke elsewhere; the sense is something rising and visible, and the choice between the two is not settled. Finally {{10.4}} with {{10.5}} says bird of wing, which is redundant on its face, and is best read as a category label rather than a description.

The problem the psalm hands a reader is that it gives orders to things that cannot hear them. Two readings answer it. One takes the summons as descriptive: a thing praises by doing what it was made to do, so the sea creature praises by being a sea creature, and verse 8 states this outright when it calls the storm wind a doer of His word. The other takes the psalm as a commission of the people who can speak, so that the list is not addressed to mountains but read aloud on their behalf, which fits its place in the morning service, where the created order is enlisted before the worshipper says anything about himself. The horn of verse 14 is read as strength restored rather than a musical instrument, and the phrase that follows it, a people near to Him, is what the whole list has been narrowing toward.

Read mystically the two halves are two worlds and the refrains are the seam between them. What is called in the first half has no body, what is called in the second half has nothing else, and the same name is praised by both, which is the claim the psalm exists to make. The descent from the waters above the heavens to the deeps below the earth traces a full column, and the ascent back through weather, growth and speech is the same column read upward, with human beings placed at the point where the column becomes articulate. The last verse gives that position a name: a people near, {{14.9}}. Nearness rather than height is the final term, and it arrives only after everything that is higher has already been called.
